analysis.one_liner: Guarantees every American Medicare-style health coverage, financed by new payroll taxes.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to three House committees and a subcommittee within a day of introduction and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended; it had 19 cosponsors, all Democrats.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a "Medicare for All" program covering every citizen and lawful resident, phased in over five years by age group. Benefits would match full Medicare hospital and doctor coverage, plus prescription drug coverage at least as broad as the Blue Cross/Blue Shield Standard plan federal employees get, mental health parity, preventive care, and home- and community-based care. People could keep choosing their own doctor or enroll in regulated private plans, and it would be paid for by a 1.7% tax on worker wages above $25,000, a 7% excise tax on employer payrolls, and a tax on self-employment income.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who lacked health coverage or couldn't afford the coverage they had — the bill entitles every eligible person to Medicare-level benefits, with reduced out-of-pocket costs for low-income people and families enrolled together on one form. Workers who currently get insurance through a job would swap employer premiums for the new payroll tax.

how_it_helps.text: Every eligible American would be entitled to Medicare-style benefits, phased in over five years starting with people under 25 or over 55, with full eligibility in the program's fifth year.

Benefits would include full Medicare parts A and B coverage, prescription drug coverage at least as comprehensive as the Blue Cross/Blue Shield Standard plan under the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program, mental health parity, preventive services, and home and community-based services.
The bill states the program must ensure all Americans have access to health care as good as their Member of Congress receives, and it requires reduced cost-sharing for low-income individuals.

People would keep their choice of doctor, and could instead enroll in private plans that must offer benefits no less than the largest Federal Employees Health Benefits plans, with the same beneficiary protections.
Workers in collectively bargained health plans would stay in those plans until their union agreements expire, rather than being moved onto the new program immediately.

analysis.who_pays: Workers would pay a 1.7% tax on wages above $25,000 (adjusted for inflation), employers would pay a 7% excise tax on the wages of enrolled employees, and self-employed people would pay both rates on their self-employment income. Cost-sharing such as deductibles and copayments would continue under Medicare-style rules, though reduced for low-income people. States could not cut Medicaid eligibility or benefits below the levels in effect when the bill was enacted.
analysis.who_pays_short: Workers and employers through payroll taxes

drawbacks.text: The bill is financed by new payroll taxes: 1.7% on wages above $25,000 for employees and 7% of wages for employers, so most working households and their employers would pay more in taxes even where the tax replaced insurance premiums, and it applies to wages rather than being tied to income beyond $25,000.
It does not eliminate out-of-pocket costs — benefits remain subject to Medicare-style deductibles, coinsurance, and copayments, plus family premiums set by the Secretary.

Coverage starts slowly: no coverage for the first 18 months after enactment, and full eligibility for all ages only in the program's fifth year, so people between 25 and 55 would wait years for entry.
Employers and unions with collectively bargained plans face a transition period in which some workers remain outside the new program until their agreements terminate.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside is large and concrete: guaranteed Medicare-level coverage for every citizen and lawful resident, with protections for low-income people and union plans, at a cost that replaces what many families and employers already spend on premiums. The honest objections are that the financing falls on wages (a 7% employer tax can be passed to workers over time), that Medicare-style deductibles and copayments survive rather than being abolished, and that the five-year phase-in delays help for working-age adults. It is a broad but gradual plan, not a single-payer bill — private insurers would keep a role inside the new program.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to three House committees on the day it was introduced and to the Ways and Means health subcommittee the next day, then sat without a hearing or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Dingell of Michigan introduced the bill on April 25, 2007, with a dozen original co-introducers including Charles Rangel, Henry Waxman, Pete Stark, and Tammy Baldwin.
It was referred the same day to the Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, and Oversight and Government Reform Committees, and referred to the Ways and Means Subcommittee on Health the next day.
Nineteen House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican did.
No committee scheduled a markup and no vote was ever held; the action history ends with the subcommittee referral, and the bill died when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

Notably, the chairs of all three committees of referral — Dingell at Energy and Commerce, Rangel at Ways and Means, and Waxman at Oversight and Government Reform — sponsored or cosponsored the bill, yet none of their committees ever took it up.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have owed the 7% payroll tax and health insurers who kept the existing employer-based system were better off because the bill died, as were lawmakers who avoided voting on a large tax increase; Americans without affordable coverage got nothing from this Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers, insurers, and the status quo

sides.party_line_note: All 19 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on, but the split never reached a vote — the bill died in committee without any member ever casting a vote for or against it.

industries.note: This is not a single-payer bill: it requires every Federal Employees Health Benefits carrier to offer a 'Medicare for All' plan with risk-adjusted per-capita payments, keeping private insurers as contracted delivery channels inside the new universal program. Universal enrollment would hand insurers a much larger guaranteed-paying market, while the default public option would compete with them.

The bill imposes a 7% excise tax on wages paid to enrolled employees, replacing (for many firms) employer health premiums with a payroll tax; collectively bargained plans are exempt until they expire. The industry's cost funds coverage its own workers would receive.

Every American would become a covered patient, ending uncompensated care, but the bill directs payment schedules to track Medicare rates, which generally pay less than private insurance. Doctors and hospitals would trade higher volumes for lower rates.

The benefit package guarantees drug coverage for everyone at least as comprehensive as the Blue Cross/Blue Shield Standard FEHBP plan, paid through a Secretary-set payment schedule. More covered patients means more insured drug demand, though public-program pricing pressure could squeeze prices.
